title: The Promise on the Bag
subtitle: A family made a pet food with one big promise on the label: “no by-product meal.” Then a competitor took them to court. What happens to a company when one promise is wrong?

vocab.def: A piece of paper on a product. It tells you what is inside.
vocab.ex: Read the label before you buy the food.

vocab.def: One of the things you use to make food.
vocab.ex: Chicken is the first ingredient in this recipe.

vocab.def: When you say very strongly that you will do something, or that something is true.
vocab.ex: The company made a promise to its customers.
This bag contains chicken and rice.

vocab.def: Not made in a factory; from plants or animals.
vocab.ex: They sell natural food for dogs.

vocab.def: A company that sells things to another company.
vocab.ex: The farm is our supplier of eggs.

vocab.def: To believe that someone is honest and will not lie to you.
vocab.ex: People trust a brand with a good name.

vocab.def: A way to check if something is true or good.
vocab.ex: A laboratory did a test on the food.

vocab.def: When one person or company takes another to court.
Something you do wrong, but you did not want to.
vocab.ex: It was a mistake, not a lie.

items: Please read the ___ on the box. It says what is inside.
Flour is the main ___ in bread.
I ___ my best friend. I can tell her anything.
A farm sells eggs to our shop. The farm is our ___.
I put salt in my tea by accident. It was a ___.
Two companies went to court. The first company started a ___.

vocab_discuss: Do you read the label when you buy food? What do you look for?
Which brands do you trust? Why?
Is “natural” food really better? What do you think?

story.heading: Part 1 — A dog called Blue
paras: In 2003, a family in the United States, the Bishops, started a pet food company. They called it Blue Buffalo.

The idea came from their dog. His name was Blue, and he was very ill with cancer. The family wanted the best food for him. They read the labels of many pet foods, and they did not like some ingredients. One of them was “by-product meal” — a cheap powder made from parts of an animal.
So they made a different food. It was natural, with real meat as the first ingredient. And on every bag, there was a big promise: no chicken by-product meal, no corn, no wheat, no soy.
The food cost more than other brands. But many owners were happy to pay. They trusted the promise — and they loved their pets.
Blue Buffalo grew very fast and became one of the best-known pet food brands in the country.
tf: The Bishops wanted by-product meal in their food.
Blue Buffalo food was cheaper than other brands.
discuss: Would you pay more for pet food with a clear promise on the bag? Why or why not?
Why do you think the family used their dog’s story in their marketing?

story.heading: Part 2 — The test
paras: In May 2014, a big competitor, Purina, started a lawsuit against Blue Buffalo.
Purina said: “Some Blue Buffalo food contains chicken by-product meal. The promise on the bag is not true.” Purina did laboratory tests on the food and took the results to court.

Blue Buffalo was in a very difficult position. A supplier had sent it the wrong ingredients and, it said, had not told the truth about them. The company did not know. It stopped buying from that supplier.
But for the customers, that did not matter. The label on the bag said “no by-product meal”, and it was not always true.
Some owners were angry. They started their own lawsuit. In the end, Blue Buffalo paid about thirty-two million dollars to settle it.
tf: Purina is a competitor of Blue Buffalo.
Blue Buffalo knew about the wrong ingredients.
Some customers also started a lawsuit.
discuss: Blue Buffalo says it did not know. Is it still responsible for the label? Why or why not?
How would you feel if you found a wrong ingredient in your food?

story.heading: Part 3 — Can you trust a promise?
paras: In November 2016, Purina and Blue Buffalo agreed to end their lawsuits. The details are secret.
The story did not end the company. Many customers kept buying Blue Buffalo. In 2018, a big food company, General Mills, bought it for about eight billion dollars.
But the story still teaches a hard lesson. A strong promise can win trust very fast — and one mistake can put that trust in danger.
The bigger the promise on the bag, the more you must check. A good company tests its ingredients and visits its suppliers. A smart customer reads the label — and asks questions.
So: was Blue Buffalo’s promise a clever idea, or a dangerous bet?
tf: The lawsuits between the two companies ended in 2016.
Customers stopped buying Blue Buffalo completely.
A bigger promise on the label needs more checking.
discuss: Was the “no by-product meal” promise a good idea? What are the good and bad points?
Tell the story again in six sentences. Use: contains, no and without.

grammar.name: no, not any, without
grammar.heading: What is in the food? contains / no / not any / without
explain: Labels say what is inside a product — and what is not inside. We use no, not any and without for this.
Something is inside: This biscuit contains chicken. / This biscuit is made with chicken.

Something is not inside — use no OR not any (same meaning):
This biscuit contains no corn.
This biscuit doesn’t contain any corn.
Never use both: This biscuit doesn’t contain no corn. ✗ — one negative is enough!
without + noun means “not having”: I like tea without sugar. / a food without artificial colours
Remember the -s: It contains chicken. (he / she / it) but The biscuits contain chicken.

practice.heading: Complete the sentences
practice.intro: Write one word in each gap: no, any, with or without.
items: This bag contains ___ corn. It says so on the label.
These biscuits don’t contain ___ artificial colours.
I drink my coffee ___ milk. I only like it black.
There isn’t ___ chicken in this soup. It is a vegetable soup.
My dog loves chicken, so I buy biscuits ___ chicken.
The laboratory found ___ problems, so the food was safe.

fix.heading: Find the mistake
items: This food doesn’t contain no corn.
I want a biscuit without of sugar.
There are not no artificial colours in it.
The food contain no by-product meal.
answers: This food doesn’t contain any corn. (or: This food contains no corn.)
This bag doesn’t contain any soy. (or: This bag contains no soy.)
There are no artificial colours in it. (or: There aren’t any artificial colours in it.)
The food contains no by-product meal. (he / she / it + -s)

speak.label: 1 · Tell the story
paras: Tell me the story in your own words. Six or seven sentences is enough.

speak.label: 2 · Read the label
paras: Here is a label: NATURAL DOG BISCUITS — contains chicken, rice and carrots. No corn. No soy. No artificial colours.
Tell me what is in the biscuits and what is not. Then say: what would you check before you believe this label?
helper: I would ask the company to…

speak.label: 3 · A promise you know
paras: Think of a product you buy: food, a drink, a phone, clothes.
What does the company promise on the box or in its advertising? Do you believe it? Why or why not?
helper: I trust / don’t trust it because…

speak.label: 4 · The difficult call
paras: Role play. Person A is a customer. Person B works for the company.
A: Your test found a wrong ingredient in the food, but the label says it is not inside. You are angry. Ask for an answer.
B: Say sorry, explain what happened and say what you will do now.
helper: It was a mistake. Our supplier…
From now on, we will test…

final: Is it a good idea to put a big promise on your product? Why or why not?
If a supplier makes a mistake, is the company responsible? Why or why not?
Which is more important for a brand: a low price, or trust? Can you give an example?
